NUMBER: 20210517
SPECIES: Northern Periodical Cicada, Magicicada septendecim Linnaeus, 1758
OTHER NAMES: 17-year cicada, Linnaeus’ periodical cicada, pharaoh cicada
DISTINCTIONS: Largest, most northern, and most famous 17-year cicada in USA.  Male posterior triangular with rounded tip not projected in peduncle.  Body black, eyes red, wings clear.
SPECIMENS: 4 adults and 3 attached tests from last (5th) molt.  Two on far right are female (left) and male (right).

DATE: 17 May 2021
LOCALITY: Falls Church, Virginia 22042

DISTRIBUTION: The Brood X (10) emergence outbreak is supposed to be occurring throughout Washington DC, southcentral through southeast Pennsylvania, extreme northern Maryland and Virginia, and northeast arm of West Virginia, USA.  The locality we report is just in the southern edge of the predicted region.
DAMAGE: They usually cause little physical damage to plants.  Their loud calls can be irritating particularly in mass.  They do not bite or sting.
USES: Spectacular emergencies of billions attract attention.  Eatable by humans.  Fed on by practicably everything but last too briefly to be of much importance.
SIMILAR SPECIES: Four species share the 17-year emergence spacing.

This is a problematic cicada! Though clearly cassinii (that's all that has emerged in my location), it has an aberrant orange patch behind its right eye. I'll be interested to see if I encounter any more like this one; it may be a rare aberration.

The answer to that question is yes. 

After 17 years in the ground, the Brood X cicada has emerged in New Jersey. 

Periodical cicadas are grouped into geographic broods based on the calendar year they emerge. In 1898, an entomologist identified 30 different broods, 17 with a 17-year life cycle and 13 with a 13-year life cycle, all of which have a Roman numeral assigned to them. 

Only 15 broods are known to have survived today, including the Brood X.

description: We heard this cicada while driving back from Farrington Lake Open Space on Farrington Blvd in a bushy overgrown area with trees near the power line cut.  We returned and recorded it. We looked a bit and did not see any cicadas or find any carapaces, but the area was very overgrown.  I would say there are not many cicadas at this location.

In Bicentennial Park and nearby Louise Drive in East Brunswick, there is a very diffuse emergence of Pharaoh Cicada - their "wee-oh" is faint and coming from "somewhere" in trees above. No individuals have been seen so far and we haven't found any carapaces yet. But they are definitely present in low numbers, generally one singing at a time but there are small clusters where one sings, then another. There are not enough to form a chorus. The song "wee-oh" is very faint on this recording , but I hope you can hear it. I put the map marker close to the part of the park where this individual was recorded.

NUMBER: 20210517
SPECIES: Northern Periodical Cicada, Magicicada septendecim Linnaeus, 1758[1]
OTHER NAMES: 17-year cicada, Linnaeus’ periodical cicada, pharaoh cicada
DISTINCTIONS: Largest, most northern, and most famous 17-year cicada in USA.  Male posterior triangular with rounded tip not projected in peduncle.  Body black, eyes red, wings clear.  Distinct orange bands on bottom (ventral) of thorax, and orange at insertion of wings behind the eyes.
BROOD: X (1749 cicadas emerging in NEUSA, Marlatt, 1923)
DATE: 17 May 2021
LOCALITY: Falls Church, Virginia 22042
LATITUDE, LONGITUDE: 38.8690, -77.1680
DISTRIBUTION: The Brood X (10) emergence outbreak is supposed to be occurring throughout Washington DC, southcentral through southeast Pennsylvania, extreme northern Maryland and Virginia, and northeast arm of West Virginia, USA.  The locality we report is just in the southern edge of the predicted region.
DAMAGE: They usually cause little physical damage to plants.  Their loud calls can be irritating particularly in mass.  They do not bite or sting.
USES: Spectacular emergencies of billions attract attention.  Eatable by humans.  Fed on by practicably everything but last too briefly to be of much importance.
SIMILAR SPECIES: Cassin’s 17-year Cicada, Magicicada cassinii (Fisher, 1852), differs by having all-black beneath the thorax instead of black with distinct orange bands, and orange instead of brown legs.  Decula 17-year Cicada, Magicicada septendecula Alexander and Moore, 1962, is smaller and rare.  It similarly has well-defined orange stripes on the underside of the abdomen but no orange coloration in front of the wing insertion behind the eye.  Riley’s 13-year Cicada, Magicicada tredecim (Walsh and Riley, 1868), is light orange to caramel on the underside of the thorax and abdomen.
COMMENT: The Alexander and Moore (1962) name M. septendecula is unfortunately very confusing in similarity.
IMPORTANCE: This is the year for mass emergence of Brood X cicadas.  Thus of use to report where and when outbreaks occur.

description: We heard Magicicada cassini calls twice when hiking a trail along Farrington Lake that parallels Farrington Lake.  The calls were far enough apart along the trail to be coming from two separate individuals. There was no continuous chorus of cicadas so these appear to be two isolated individuals. We have recorded M. cassini and M. septendecim at other locations, but did not have recording equipment with us today. The first set of calls we heard consisted of a loud pulsing and the second set of calls included the characteristic few seconds of clicking followed by loud pulses of sound. This was not the "wee-oh" of  the Pharaoh cicada, nor was it the sound of annual cicadas. crickets, etc. The pulsing can also be described like a brief "revving" of a chain saw. The clicking was absolutely like what we have heard from Cassini cicadas in other locations.

description: This appeared to be the waning end of the Great Eastern Brood aka Brood X of the 17-year cicadas. They were still plentiful but the locals said they weren't as thick any more as they had been just a couple of days earlier, so probably past peak in this location. There may have been more than one species in the area based on the songs I heard (or maybe I was just imagining that), but it appeared the predominant one - and all the cicadas I picked up and looked at - were the Magicicada cassinii type with entirely black abdomen. The sound files have some birds mixed in with the cicada chorus. The photos and sound files in this observation were recorded along the edge of the woods with trees on one side of the path and a hay field on the other side. The exuviae and individuals photographed were all crawling on the shrubby vegetation along the forest edge. Also see the following observations that are part of this set: Male - https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/83981587 Female - https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/83981813 Exuviae - https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/83982431 Video footage: https://youtu.be/xxn0UUOlan8

description:
It would be interesting to see cicadas Brood X evolution tree. They are truly bezoar insects. They have 5 eyes to navigate the above ground world. 2 compound eyes and 3 ocellus. The term "ocellus" (plural ocelli) is derived from the Latin world oculus (eye), and literally means "little eye".

I'm assuming their eyes are very similar to Australian ‘Redeye’ cicada-Psaltoda moerens eyes. The Research School of Biology at Australian National University did a study in 2015 and discovered in the red eye cicada 8 retinular cells form a fused rhabdom. They noted in particular that cicadas are the only Hemipteran group with fused rhabdoms, thus making Hemiptera an interesting case to study the evolution of open rhabdoms and neural superposition. 

The compound eyes have large visual fields, about 7500 ommatidia per eye. These tube like Structures remind me of the spore surface of polypore mushrooms. That black spot in their eyes that appears to be always looking at you is really you looking down the structured like tubes of their ommatidia. They have binocular overlaps of 10-15° in the frontal and of 50-60° in the dorsal visual field. The diameters of corneal facet lenses range between 22 and 34 μm and the lenses are unusually long with up to 100 μm in some eye regions. In the posterior part of the eyes, the hexagonal facet array changes to a square lattice. The compound eyes are of the eucone apposition type with 8 retinular cells contributing to a fused rhabdom in each ommatidium. The red eye colour is due to the pigment granules in the secondary pigment cells. They found a small Dorsal Rim Area (DRA), in which rhabdom cross-sections are rectangular rather than round. The cross-sections of DRA rhabdoms do not systematically change orientation along the length of the rhabdom, indicating that microvilli directions do not twist, which would make retinular cells in the DRA polarization sensitive.

The three ocelli have unusual lenses with a champagne-cork shape in longitudinal sections. Retinular cells are short in the dorsal and ventral part of the retinae, and long in their equatorial part. Ocellar rhabdoms are short (<10 μm), positioned close to the corneagenous layer and are formed by pairs of retinular cells. In cross-section, the rhabdomeres are 2-5 μm long and straight. The red color of ocelli is produced by screening pigments that form an iris around the base of the ocellar lens and by screening pigments between the ocellar retinular cells.

description: Happy Wing Wednesday! I was chasing another insect in my yard (Durham NC USA) when this cicada came out of some vegetation and perched on a tree. I got a few images before it flew off. Periodical Cicada - Magicicada species bugguide.net/node/view/6970 Having watched insects for 30 years in this area, I have seen periodical cicadas only in years when brood XIX (a 13-year brood) is expected: 1998 and 2011. They are expected back in spring 2024. My best guess is that this is an off-year emergent of brood XIX. Also posted at: bugguide.net/node/view/2113493 In one frame I can just see that the underside of the abdomen is tan, so this is most likely: Riley's 13-year Cicada - Magicicada tredecim bugguide.net/node/view/511588 Edit. There is also an orange mark on the edge of the pronotum, another character for tredecim. Thinking back to 2011, this was the only species I found emerging in my yard. (The other common one in the area in 2011 was M. tredecassini, which has a mostly dark abdomen.)

UPDATE 6/12: I got a better recording, which I've added here and is now the first file. 

Poor recording, for which I apologize. The tragedies of living on a busy suburban street; loud neighbors, overhead planes, cars, and an inconvenient catbird. The sound pollution we live with on a daily basis is astounding...
One, potentially two, though I couldn't be certain, M. septendecim individual(s) singing from across the street for about two hours on and off. It was faint but clear and unmistakable, even though it came out a lot less clear in the recordings. I don't think it was far away - possibly just 50-100 ft from where I was standing. I heard it as soon as I walked out the door and had to stand there listening to make sure I wasn't imagining things! I am outside in the yard every day and this is the first time I've heard it. 
Hard to pick out in the recordings I realize, as it's sort of an ambient drone, but best heard when it drops off the first time at 00:13 in the first recording. That dropoff can be heard less clearly another two times in the second recording.

The serendipity of finding not one, but now two unexpected Magicicada stragglers this year when not at all looking for them really makes me believe there are many more out there just not being detected!

The sound of the summer of 2016, here in western Pennsylvania, U.S.A., was definately dominated by the  return of the 17-year Cicadas! A few days later, I thought I heard one alone in the morning, and by mid-day it was apparent that the invasion was truly on - and seemed at first to be coming, slowly, gradually, over the hill east of our Buffalo Township farmhouse. 

We have since often called their chorus "deafening," which is quite true in the sense that they drown out almost all the other sounds that we are used to hearing this time of year. They even make conversation difficult outdoors. A friend memorably observed that together, they make exactly the sound of the original  Star Trek Enterprise's main phasers! 

These 17-year Pharaoh Cicadas are very unlike the larger ones heard most intervening summers, both physically and audibly. Turn your speakers down some if you want, there was no way to quiet this loud chorus in the field! 

Listen carefully and you'll hear some other pretty interesting bird and insect sounds embedded in the Cicada chorus.

Brood X / “The Great Eastern Brood” emergence of 17-year cicadas in 2021. While observing them we tried to document signs of the specialized pathogenic “zombie fungus,” Massospora cicadina, that destroys periodical cicadas’ abdomens while altering their mating instincts. I’m not sure which of the 3 Magicicada species I was observing but I believe the ones on this tree to be M. septendecim, as they were larger than others we found on closeby plants.

Site at White Clay Creek State Park that was very active during the emergence of the Brood X periodicals. All three local species were heard: M. septendecim, M. cassini, and M. septendecula. However, only M. septendecim specimens were directly observed.

I don’t know how to differentiate between the 3 Magicicada species but am uploading these as a separate observation to a similar one I posted, as these cicadas were found in a different area of the same park. The cicadas that were climbing up this tree and were in the immediate surrounding areas seemed smaller than others we saw in some nearby trees, but it’s possibly due to the fact that these ones were in a very dry, hot, intensely sunny spot and many of their wings did not unfurl fully or dry correctly. There seemed to be a disproportionate amount of little flightless cicadas on the ground and crawling on rocks in this spot because one or both of their wings were malformed / dried crumpled. I don’t know enough about cicada morphology or behavior to make a call on the species, but of the many I witnessed, these seem most like they could be M. cassinii due to their small size and vivid orange wings.

description: Riley's 13-year Cicada - Magicicada tredecim (female, body length 29 mm) Location: Durham NC (USA) I picked up a freshly-emerged pair for detailed photos. Female has no visible sound-producing organs at the base of the abdomen. In cicadas, sound-sensing organs are in the legs, apparently--see: Alt and Harlan. Sensing of Substrate Vibrations in the Adult Cicada Okanagana rimosa (Hemiptera: Cicadidae). J Insect Sci. 2018 May 1;18(3):16. doi: 10.1093/jisesa/iey029. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29893892/ I see reports that females of some cicada species do have tymbals, but I would like to see confirmation of that in the scientific literature. Reading popular accounts, it seems there is some confusion about tymbals being used for sensing sounds. I think that is incorrect, and they are the sound producing organs only. There are smaller organs for sensing sounds. Edit. These cicadas are alive--I chilled them briefly in my refrigerator so I could get detailed images of the underside, which is otherwise difficult. I released them after they warmed up.

description:
Riley's 13-year Cicada - Magicicada tredecim (teneral female)
Location: Durham NC (USA)
They continue to climb up a tree in my front yard at dusk. A few molt out of their last nymph skin where I can see them. Caught this one at the pretty stage where the pale wings inflate and expand sideways. A little later, and they fold against the body.
Note on species ID:
Even molting nymphs of tredecim in this area are recognizable by the size--body length ~27-29 mm (male/female) and the body is quite plump. The other common species, M. tredecassini, is 20-23 mm with a thin body. The last, of three in this area, is M. tredecula. It is uncommon--I saw just a few in 2011, and not around my home. It is even smaller than tredecassini.
Here I photographed the shed skin of this same individual next morning, and it is almost 30mm.

Native to the USA and Canada, the Pharaoh Cicada is the largest of the periodical cicadas. It is also the northernmost. Its life cycyle is 17 years in length. The name comes from its call which some say resemples the word 'pharaoh'.

description: Point G
mating pair of Magicicada cassini

Magicicada septendecim, photographed (and held) to clearly display the visual differences in the abdomen that most easily distinguish them from the simultaneous brood of Magicicada cassini! This individual is male: note the lack ovipositor at the end of the abdomen in the second photo.

He was quite irked at my audacity to not in fact be some manner of tree or shrub like he had hoped to land on, and performed his distinctive scream very admirably; at this point in the emergence, they are active but clumsy fliers, and large numbers that have mated are beginning to die off naturally.

description:
I seem to be observing members of brood XIV (Bourbon Brood). 

My first sighting was two days ago on May 17th, at Broad Run Park. I and one of my buddies saw several that had fallen into the river we were wading in and had helped them onto the snags and trees along the banks. Later that evening, I found a multitude of husks under the birch trees in my yard. On May 18th, I saw 3 more individuals while fishing at McNeely Lake. Today (May 19th) I found two forewings and a hindwing under the birches, as well as more husks.

I never had the opportunity to measure any of them, but I would say they were all about 1.5 inches in length from the head to the tip of the wings when folded.

description:
May 24, OVNARGS garden tour in New Richmond, Ohio (right along the Ohio River):
I've heard that 17-year cicadas are emerging in the area, but emergence seems to be patchy and isn't happening right where I live. However, during a garden tour with the Ohio Valley Chapter of the North American Rock Garden Society (OVNARGS), I spotted this freshly drowned individual in a wheelbarrow that had collected rainwater. I also saw one shell, and the homeowner said he'd seen a few, too. They weren't singing like crazy and there weren't a zillion exit holes in the soil, though, so either emergence is just starting or this place was only on the edge of a big brood area. The property had many huge, old trees, so it should have been good habitat for the nymphs.

description:
In the boulevard island in front of the National Exemplar, Mariemont: This is a really interesting location, because the giant ash trees that lined the center of the boulevard were all removed in 2010 because of the emerald ash borer. This was only two years after the 2008 emergence of Brood XIV here, and we expected that the nymphs would have died after the loss of the trees. New trees (Chinese elms) were planted during 2010, but obviously the transition took some time, leaving the nymphs without a source of xylem fluid in the interim.

However, the 2008 nymphs survived with or without those tree roots, and here they are, emerging in good numbers (though not as prodigious as in the previous generation).
